entries.title: Emmy highlights: Mariska Hargitay sings, Taylor Swift acts in a skit and Jean Smart wins
entries.summary: <p>The Emmy Awards are underway. “The Pitt” and “Widow’s Bay” are generating buzz as they compete for top prizes. The ceremony is also honoring the anniversaries of “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” and “Charlie’s Angels.”</p><p>Here are some highlights as the show roars into the night.</p><h3>The host with the mostest</h3><h3></h3><p>Mariska Hargitay kicked off the show with New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson in an exuberant and looney pre-taped bit that had her sing a version of “I Love Rock ’n’ Roll” by Joan Jett & the Blackhearts, renamed “I Love TV Screens” as she flew from New York to Los Angeles.</p><p>The first-time Emmy host was then seen relaxed in bed with “Hacks” star Jean Smart, ate a burger in a nod to “Beef,” rode a horse and drank bubble tea with Jennifer Coolidge.</p><p>On stage, she reveled in the fact that she was the first woman to host in 15 years. The star of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit,” entering its 28th season, also joked that she’s never had to pronounce the word “finale” and even seemed to swipe the script for Nicole Kidman’s kitschy AMC ad, which drew Kidman’s mock ire.</p><p>She said she got two pieces of advice: “No. 1, don’t do it, and No. 2, whatever you do, don’t go for sincerity,” she said. “I clearly ignored the first, so please join me as I ignore the second.”</p><p>“She crushed it,” said Amy Poehler, who took the stage after the opening.</p><h3>Taylor Swift was there, kind of</h3><h3></h3><p>In a pre-taped sketch, Taylor Swift played a rookie in “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” as the cops got a bit looney.</p><p>Hargitay’s Olivia Benson went through two large crime boards to make connections between Swift’s songs and Emmy nominations to see if she’d attend the Emmys. One of the detectives called it a “rabbit hole.”</p><p>“Those categories were last week. Why would she be showing up to the ceremony tonight? She’s probably going to be sitting at home playing with those cats she’s named after TV show characters,” Swift’s unnamed character scoffs.</p><p>Hargitay concludes: “Taylor Swift will not be at the Emmys.” Swift offers another option: “Maybe she’ll do one those cool, pre-taped sketch things to support the host.”</p><p>The sketch ends with Hargitay posing with Swift — both glaring into the camera, very seriously — bookmarking Swift’s cat, named in tribute of Olivia Benson.</p><h3>The Smart money</h3><h3></h3><p>Jean Smart was predicted to win her fifth straight Emmy for “Hacks” and did it with style. “What a ride this has been,” she said.</p><p>It’s her eighth trophy overall, which ties the all-time performer record shared by Cloris Leachman, Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Allison Janney who also won Monday. Smart also becomes the first woman to win best actress for each season of a show’s run.</p><p>Smart, 75, who first got noticed in the CBS comedy “Designing Women,” won her first Emmys for guest appearances on “Frasier” and then another for a supporting role on “Samantha Who.”</p><p>On Monday, she kept a special thank you to the end — “Hacks” creators Lucia Aniello, Paul W. Downs and Jen Statsky: “It all begins and ends with them,” she said.</p><h3>‘Buffy’ turns 30</h3><h3></h3><p>Just six months after the “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” reboot was scrapped, stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz reunited onstage to celebrate the show’s 30th anniversary.</p><p>After Boreanaz mused whether their characters, Buffy and Angel, would ever get together, Gellar had a sharp retort referencing the cancellation.</p><p>“Guess we’ll never find out!” Gellar said.</p><p>She also acknowledged it had been a tough two years for the show’s cast and crew, implicitly acknowledging the recent deaths of actors Anthony Head (Giles), Nicholas Brendon (Xavier) and Michelle Trachtenberg (Dawn).</p><h3>Welcome back, Sofia</h3><h3></h3><p>Sofia Vergara made it to the Emmys this year to present supporting actor in a comedy, bypassing the emergency room. Last year, she had to bow out of presenting at the last minute after suffering an eye allergy just before the show.</p><h3>Pre-show chaos</h3><h3></h3><p>In the hour before the show opens, the Peacock Theater lobby was as jammed as an LA freeway.</p><p>Women wearing long trains attempt to protect them from an errant shoe as guests bump elbows and brush backs trying to make their way across the lobby. It’s time to gird for the three-hour show ahead, which means buying $9 cups of popcorn, $8 hot dogs and $23 beers and cocktails to carry to seats. It doesn’t appear nachos are a popular item — too messy for folks in tuxes and gowns</p><h3>One person dressed appropriately</h3><h3></h3><p>Meg Stalter, a nominee for best supporting actress for “Hacks,” was dressed as an Emmy statuette, complete with wings and a coat of gold makeup. She even held up a sphere like the real trophy itself.</p><p>It was Stalter’s first time attending the Emmys as a nominee. She earned her first career nod for supporting actress in a comedy series for playing Kayla Schaeffer in the fifth and final season of “Hacks.”</p><h3>Small tables and lamps</h3><p>Similar to the Grammys held across the street, this year the Emmys are having the biggest names seated at small tables with lamps on them in front of the stage.</p><p>Typically, the guests are seated in long rows like a movie theater. There’s still the same pre-show hobnobbing. It seems no one wants to sit down early, knowing they’ll be in those seats for the next three hours.</p>

entries.title: Cubs see Alex Bregman being himself, rather than his ample playoff experience, as difference-maker in October
entries.summary: <p><b>Alex Bregman</b> has played in a lot of playoff games.</p><p>Like a lot.</p><p>In fact, he’s ninth all time, having appeared in 102 of them.</p><p>The two-time World Series champion would obviously like to add a third ring to his fingers this year, his first after signing a $175 million free-agent deal with the Cubs last offseason.</p><p>He didn’t get that contract because of his postseason experience, rather because he’s a really good baseball player regardless of the month, and he’s shown it in the second half of this season; he brought a 1.029 OPS in his previous 55 games into Monday, all <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/05/cubs-alex-bregman-defense-gold-glove-ryan-zeferjahn-save-javier-assad-marlins" >while playing Gold Glove type defense at third base</a>.</p><p>The Cubs don’t expect Bregman to start doing anything differently once the calendar flips to October. And that’s exactly what they’ll need in order to keep <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/11/cubs-best-offense-worst-pitching-baseball-alex-bregman-stats-dansby-swanson-injury-edward-cabrera" >their best-in-baseball lineup</a> humming and give themselves a chance at a deep postseason run.</p><p>“Alex is going to keep being Alex and just be relentless and try to beat you,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Monday. “He’s just going to keep doing it, no matter what’s going on. That’s what he’s great at. That just leads to success, it just does.</p><p>“Sometimes, we make a lot of experience at this time of year. And it’s important, but it’s not mandatory. I can list off tons of examples of guys who have had unbelievable postseasons without experience.</p><p>“But Alex is just who he is. ‘I’m going to beat you.’ That’s just who he is. That’s how he wakes up. If he sleeps, that’s how he goes to sleep. I’m not sure that he sleeps. But that’s who he is.”</p><p>Of course, taking the eighth most at-bats, scoring the sixth most runs and hitting the seventh most homers in postseason history has to be good for something, right?</p><p>Even if it just means that you’ve been a good player on a successful team, Bregman — lauded all season long for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-alex-bregman-home-run-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-pitcher-mlb-trade-deadline-angels" >aiding teammates with off-field conversations</a> — figures to be able to help his team when the lights get their brightest.</p><p>“Alex has performed on the biggest stage over his career, time and time again. His experience there benefits all of us,” lefty pitcher <b>Matthew Boyd</b> said. “And he’s just an overall great hitter, and he continues to get better.</p><p>“It’s a guy you’re super grateful to have on your team. The way he can attack and prepare just makes us all better.”</p><h3><b>Playoff preview?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>With the NL wild-card race still capable of turning out a number of different ways, this week’s series between the Cubs and Braves is a potential preview of a first-round postseason matchup.</p><p>Regardless of whether the two clash in October, though, it’s a meeting of two of the league’s top contending teams as each tries to tune up for lengthy playoff runs, the type of testing the Cubs need as they look to lock down a wild-card spot over the regular season’s final couple weeks.</p><p>“There’s a benefit to be playing good times at this time of year,” Boyd said. “It prepares you for what is ahead. That’s been the case with us. We’ve got good competition.”</p><h3><b>Wheels Kelly</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Cubs catcher <b>Carson Kelly</b> is his team’s second slowest player, so says his 25.8-feet-per-second sprint speed measured by Statcast.</p><p>But no one told him that as he ran his way to a couple Cubs runs in the second inning Monday.</p><p>With the bases loaded, Kelly beat out what might have been an inning-ending double-play ball, allowing a run to score and keeping the inning alive for <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>, who doubled into the right-field corner, Kelly scoring all the way from first base.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">wait, we have two more! <a href="https://t.co/RFeMs8HO0s">pic.twitter.com/RFeMs8HO0s</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2099653212882018528?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 15, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions for now ahead of midterms
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — The <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court" target="_blank" >Supreme Court</a> on Monday rejected President <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/donald-trump" target="_blank" >Donald Trump’s</a> bid to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already underway.</p><p>The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they’ve used for years. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented from the brief order.</p><p>“The court’s decision is a victory for voters, for democracy and for the rule of law in this country," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, who was part of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/26/illinois-ag-kwame-raoul-lawsuit-postal-service-mail-ballot-rule-midterm-elections" >lawsuit challenging the proposed measure</a>. "The courts have recognized that states do not have the time to completely overhaul their mail-in ballot procedures to comply with a Postal Service rule that is unlawful in the first place. If allowed to go into effect, this rule would have created chaos and undermined confidence in our upcoming general election."</p><p>The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail.</p><p>The Supreme Court majority did not detail its reasoning, as is typical on the high court’s emergency docket. Alito, meanwhile, said in the dissent that the Postal Service “has broad authority to regulate the mail” and likely does have the power to enforce Trump’s restrictions.</p><p>Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed the restrictions should not go into effect for the midterms but indicated he might rule in favor of the Trump administration if the issue comes back before the court.</p><p>Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active.</p><p>The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn’t comply.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/midterm-elections-postal-service-mail-voting-7f7cf4fdf2e9cf369ae96f96fbda03f2" target="_blank" >whistleblower report</a>, though, said the postal system’s requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn’t properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out.</p><p>Democratic state officials and voting rights groups <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/election-2026-trump-mail-voting-postal-service-ce207ff2d0533de05cc2d299e91a0198" target="_blank" >challenged the restrictions</a> in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election.”</p><p>Lower courts agreed and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-executive-order-midterms-3e2c89ab0a0f7faca75e50ff34adee15" target="_blank" >blocked Trump’s plan</a>, including <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-executive-order-midterms-906aa1247f096609e61a1bd2369a57e9" target="_blank" >a preliminary injunction</a> issued by a judge nominated by the president.</p><p>But the Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that federal control of the Postal Service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible.</p><p>The federal government won an <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-supreme-court-157afc3c195ce0a62c522da5ce904b04" target="_blank" >early procedural decision</a> at the Supreme Court, but the justices pointedly did not rule on the legality of the plan.</p><p>Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module entries.title: Lawmakers name acting legislative inspector general after McCuskey resignation
entries.summary: <p>A former federal prosecutor who investigated crimes against humanity committed by Saddam Hussein will be tasked with probing allegations of misconduct by Illinois lawmakers beginning next month.</p><p>The bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission named David Risley acting legislative inspector general effective Oct. 1, taking the place of Michael McCuskey, who last week <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/09/08/mike-mccuskey-resigns-benton-report-investigation-complaint" target="_blank" ><u>announced his resignation</u></a> at the end of the month in the wake of complaints about his handling of sexual harassment allegations that have roiled Springfield.</p><p>Risley, who previously worked as an investigator under former Legislative Inspector General Carol Pope, was an assistant U.S. attorney for Illinois’ central district, and he served in the U.S. Regime Crimes Liaison Office investigating crimes against humanity in Iraq.</p><p>Risley is also a former ethics officer for the state Department of Transportation who has maintained a part-time adviser role in the inspector general's office, and he has hosted a podcast We are committed to ensuring the highest ethical standards are enforced and that all complainants, respondents and witnesses are given the due process and consideration they deserve."</p><p>Risley becomes the newest face of an office that has failed to rein in Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment — largely because lawmakers haven’t given it the teeth to independently oversee the Capitol.</p><p>When she stepped down as legislative inspector general in 2021, Pope dismissed the post as “essentially a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/7/14/22578069/watchdog-legislative-inspector-general-carol-pope-ethics-reforms-illinois-legislature" target="_blank" ><u>paper tiger</u></a>” and declared “true ethics reform is not a priority” for lawmakers.</p><p>Ethics experts have long called for changes to state law to allow the legislative inspector general to issue subpoenas and publish reports without the approval of the ethics commission, which includes eight lawmakers.</p><p>Risley can serve until the current inspector general term ends in mid-2028, but the ethics commission is seeking applicants to take on the permanent role well before then.</p>

entries.title: No injuries after 12-year-old fires gun left unattended on school bus in Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p>No one was injured after a child fired a gun left aboard a school bus in Bridgeport Monday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Police said a man left a bag with a loaded gun unattended on the bus in the 3500 block of South Wallace Street — the same block as Minnie Miñoso Academy. A 12-year-old boy found the gun, and fired once. The bullet hit a window of the bus; no injuries were reported.</p><p>The man then took the gun and bag and fled the scene, police said. The incident is under investigation.</p>

entries.title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ breaks Emmys comedy record with 14 wins including best comedy series
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — “Widow’s Bay” stormed the Emmy Awards on Monday night, breaking a record for a comedy series with 14 awards including best comedy series and three acting wins.</p><p>The first-season horror comedy created by Katie Dippold about a New England island community reckoning with a centuries-old curse spoiled the going-away party for “Hacks,” which had gotten the most comedy nominations of any show in its fifth and final season.</p><p>It broke the comedy record set last year by “The Studio” when it won 13.</p><p>It also won for directing for Hiro Murai and for writing for its creator Dippold, a first-time Emmy winner and first-time nominee who was previously best known for an old viral tweet showing her dressed as “The Babadook.”</p><p>Star Matthew Rhys won best actor, Stephen Root won best supporting actor and Kate O’Flynn won best supporting actress. Dippold won for writing.</p><p>“The celebrations will be long, varied, and I hope at times wild,” Rhys said backstage while holding both Emmys.</p><p>It also won for directing for Hiro Murai and for writing for its creator Dippold, a first-time Emmy winner and first-time nominee who was previously best known for an old viral tweet showing her dressed as “The Babadook.”</p><p>“The Late Show with Stephen Colbert,” taken off the air by CBS, won best variety series. It’s one of six Emmys the show has won this year after the show was canceled for what the network said was economic reasons while many believe it was his criticism of the Trump administration.</p><p>“If you like the comedy tonight, my old writers wrote it,” said Colbert, who graduated from Northwestern University and cut his comedy teeth at Chicago's Second City and now chairs its board of directors.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-880000" entries.title: Tristan Peters' 18-pitch walk, baserunning play and 'dumb stuff' key crucial White Sox victory in Cleveland
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — General manager Chris Getz, having flown in Monday for the start of the White Sox’ three-game series, said there were only “minimal” reasons they couldn’t stop their slide of 10 losses in 14 games, which had shaved their American League Central lead over the Guardians to a half-game.</p><p>Manager Will Venable and his staff posted photos of Sox season highlights on the wall of the tunnel between the visitors’ locker room and the dugout at Progressive Field.</p><p>If the visual aids weren’t enough, the Sox’ coaching staff reiterated in pregame meetings the importance of the relaxed, fun vibe that had powered this young team to its surprising postseason opportunity.</p><p>But how does a roster filled with players who never had been in a game as meaningful as the one Monday — a 7-3 victory that clinched the season series and secured the tiebreaker over the Guardians in the division — force itself to relax?</p><p>“We’re saying dumb stuff,” outfielder Tristan Peters said. “We’ve got guys like [pitcher Mike] Vasil who really get us fired up and really focused on having fun with each other.”</p><p>After weeks of frustration, wayward pitching, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/13/white-sox-spurn-david-sandlins-brilliance-scoring-opportunities-in-rubber-match-loss-colson-montgomery-error-will-venable-chris-murphy-kyle-teel-shane-murphy-brian-bannister" target="_blank" ><u>repeated failures with the bases loaded</u></a> and five scoreless innings Monday against fireballing Guardians right-hander Gavin Williams, Peters sparked the Sox with the sort of dumb stuff only a gritty team could conjure.</p><p>After falling behind 1-2 in the count against Williams (13-8), who was nearing 100 pitches with no outs in the top of the sixth, Peters choked up with two strikes and fouled off a high fastball, then a low curve, a sweeper and another heater. He took ball two, then resumed fouling pitches off — 12 in all.</p><p>“I counted at one point, and I just stopped counting because it was getting up there,” Williams told reporters afterward.</p><p>Said Peters: “It felt like I was up there for, like, an hour. I swung at one that might have hit me.”</p><p>Williams’ 18th pitch in the longest major-league plate appearance of the season was a backdoor curve that missed for a walk, ending his night at 113 pitches. As Peters jogged to the dugout during the pitching change, his teammates were gleeful.</p><p>“I loved it,” left fielder Sam Antonacci said. “I think I was more happy than he was.”</p><p>With Colson Montgomery batting a play later, Peters experienced what he described as “the greatest feeling in the world” — first baseman Nathaniel Lowe’s throw on a potential double-play ball caroming off his helmet and into the outfield for a run-scoring error.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tristan Peters called getting conked in the head with a throw “one of the greatest feelings ever” <a href="https://t.co/ubo8dK0UJL">pic.twitter.com/ubo8dK0UJL</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2099687545546187215?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 15, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Chase Meidroth followed with an RBI single. Two batters later, pinch hitter Randal Grichuk loaded the bases with a knock of his own. And in the wake of the Sox going 1-for-13 with the bases loaded in their last 14 games, Kyle Teel exorcised those demons with a two-run double. By the time Miguel Vargas launched a two-run home run to cap a back-breaking six-run frame, the Sox were doing their silly dugout celebrations again.</p><p>“We have a team here that kind of thrives in that environment,” said winning pitcher Sean Burke (9-7), making a claim that sounded much more credible after his five innings without an earned run.</p><p>His key for bouncing back from the worst outing of his career?</p><p>“Just trying to throw the ball as hard as I can right down the middle,” Burke said. “I found that helps me just get back and be simple.”</p><p>There were dumb mistakes, too. All three Guardians runs were unearned.</p><p>Venable tried not to celebrate the Sox claiming the tiebreaker; they’re 1½ games ahead now but still could leave Cleveland in second place. But his team was happy about something that went beyond the standings.</p><p>“That [game] was more like ourselves,” Peters said.</p>

entries.title: Hall of Famer Drew Brees' comment in production meeting stuck with Bears QB Caleb Williams in Panthers game
entries.summary: <p>Television production meetings are a way for broadcasters to get information from players and coaches ahead of calling their game, but it worked the other direction in this case.</p><p>It just so happened for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams that Fox assigned Adam Amin, Drew Brees and Kristina Pink to his team's opener Sunday at the Panthers, and something Brees said to Williams during the week truly landed. Brees stressed to Williams the importance of taking the easy ones and checking down, and coach Ben Johnson considered that a contribution to his preparation.</p><p>"Caleb and I were talking about it the night before the game, just his conversation with Drew Brees," Johnson said Monday. "The difference between 60% and 70% [completions], he said the difference is three completions a game. Then you turn on our tape and... that might've stuck with our guy a little bit, which was cool to see.</p><p>"A couple checkdowns to the backs were good plays for us. There's a couple of times where the primary's not there and you can see him reset to the middle of the field where No. 2 was, and he ended up dotting that for five-yard gains a couple times. He had some really nice throwaways when the plays weren't there. He was smart with the football."</p><p>Johnson set completing 70% of his passes as the standard for Williams, so he must have loved Williams hearing that from someone else for a change. Brees completed 67.7% for his career (No. 3 in NFL history), including seven seasons of 70% or better. His 74.4% in 2018 is the all-time record, followed by his 74.3% the next season.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" >Williams was sharp in the Bears’ 59-37 win</a>. He completed 21 of 29 passes, and to Brees' point, that was 72.4%, whereas three fewer completions would've been 62.1%. Only two of those incomplete passes were poorly thrown, with most being throwaways. He finished with 269 yards passing, two touchdown passes and a 124.1 passer rating in addition to rushing for 65 yards and two touchdowns.</p><p>On passes thrown within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage, Williams completed 14 of 15. He also connected on three passes thrown more than 20 yards downfield from the line of scrimmage.</p><p>Brees' impact on the Bears began indirectly when he was inducted into the Hall of Fame last month. Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen and offensive line coach Dan Roushar attended the ceremony, and Johnson had them address the team about it when they returned.</p><p>“They go to the Hall of Fame acceptance speech for Drew Brees, and to me, it’s a reminder of why we get into what we do as coaches," Johnson told the Sun-Times. "Yeah, sure, we want to win games and Super Bowls and all that just like everybody else on the team, but our coaching ‘why’ is really to see these guys become the best versions of themselves.</p><p>"That’s a cliché, but when you watch and listen to those Hall of Fame speeches and you have coaches that are present and they were asked there by the athlete, that’s what’s impactful to me. I took this job [because] I wanted the chance to take a young quarterback and help shape, mold and pour whatever I could into him. That’s what I want to do on a daily basis and a yearly basis. That’s what’s been really rewarding."</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Drama queen disrupts gatherings without even being there
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A good friend in our prayer circle, "Diane," has a friend, "Suzy," with whom several of us once socialized. We've all distanced ourselves because Suzy has anger and stability issues that have become increasingly frequent since her former spouse has begun dating again. Diane allows Suzy to verbalize all kinds of half-truths and act out with volatile behavior, which some of us feel is basically encouraging destructive mental health.</p><p>While some of us suspect Diane enjoys the drama of recounting Suzy's latest issue, others believe she thinks she's "being there" for Suzy. Since so much of each meeting is now focusing on Diane's description of Suzy's latest tantrum, how can we encourage her to help Suzy get the counseling she needs to get past not only her divorce, but also the results of several years of negative behavior, and focus on the real reason we are gathering? — <i>CARING FRIEND IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRIEND:</b> Has it occurred to you that instead of praying, which is what those meetings are supposed to be about, Diane has hijacked the purpose of the meeting with gossip when she describes in detail poor Suzy's antics? What an invasion of Suzy's privacy! Tell Diane that if she really wants to help her friend, she should encourage her to get professional help and, if she's reluctant to do it, to pray (as will you all!) that Suzy summons up the courage.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I live in a neighborhood that has no sidewalks, and I vacation in a busy coastal area that also has narrow roads. My dog and I walk at least once a day along these roads, and I've noticed that many pedestrians don't know which side of the road to walk down.</p><p>According to the Scouts, you should walk facing traffic. This makes sense because you can see vehicles coming toward you and can move out of the way if they do not or cannot move around you. These days, electric cars are so quiet that many walkers don't hear them coming. Driving when you never know where walkers will be is dangerous, too. Please get the word out to walk or jog facing traffic, but not down the middle of the road. Thanks! — <i>DOG WALKER IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR WALKER:</b> I have long thought that my column serves as a sort of extended "community billboard." Your safety message is an important one. Thank you for taking the time to share it.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We need advice on the polite thing to do when you observe something on the face of a person you are talking to. Should you: a) Motion with your finger on your face that an object has been observed; b) Tell the person discreetly; c) Say or do nothing? Does it make a difference if the person is a friend, spouse or casual acquaintance? In the case of a spouse or good friend, should the observer suggest removing it? Does the same thing apply if you notice a zipper undone, button unfastened, clothing untucked, a smudge, tear or wet spot? — <i>DIFFERENT OPINIONS</i></p><p><b>DEAR OPINIONS:</b> I think the kind choice would be to inform the person of the problem discreetly, which would cause the least confusion and embarrassment. If appropriate, offer to help and see if it is welcome.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: How Bears RB D'Andre Swift became exactly the type of runner coach Ben Johnson needs
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson gets peppered constantly about whether <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >he and quarterback Caleb Williams are on the same wavelength</a>. It’s understandable, given how critical their connection is.</p><p>But Johnson was, is and always will be a run-first offensive mind. With the utmost craftsmanship, he pours himself into studying and designing run plays. And for those plays to click, much like with Williams in the passing attack, Johnson and his running back must share a vision.</p><p>Which brings us to the curious case of how D’Andre Swift went from being a player the Lions traded away when Johnson was their offensive coordinator to an indispensable piece for Johnson’s Bears.</p><p>Neither Swift nor Johnson has ever shared much about the parting of ways in Detroit in 2023 — Swift is quiet in general — but in their fifth season together, it’s clear the two have merged mentally. Swift has gifts Johnson wants to magnify. Johnson’s plays work best if Swift follows them.</p><p>Johnson said Monday he’s confident in how Swift sees plays, evidence of lockstep thinking that Swift demonstrated Sunday in the Bears’ 59-37 victory as he shredded the Panthers for one of the top 10 games of his career: 124 yards and three touchdowns on just 18 carries.</p><p>“[There were] some things that came up in the game that aren’t exactly how we coach it,” Johnson said. “Yet when I watch it, I see his perspective. ‘I would like you to cut it up there, but I see the [open space] that you’re seeing, so I understand why you bounced [outside] instead.’</p><p>“There’s a lot of back and forth, and the more we’re together and the more we talk through it, the better we’re going to be.”</p><p>Swift was tremendous last season, with a career-high 1,087 yards rushing, and is off to a fantastic start in this one, so the partnership certainly is headed in the right direction. Johnson said Swift’s work ethic is “exactly what we want to be about.”</p><p>However, it was logical to be skeptical about this pairing when the Bears hired Johnson in January 2025. As the Lions’ coordinator, he’d moved on to Jahmyr Gibbs at running back and created an overwhelming rushing attack around Gibbs and David Montgomery. Swift made the Pro Bowl in his only season with the Eagles, then landed a hefty free-agent deal from the Bears under the previous coaching staff. After his career-low 3.8 yards per carry in 2024, the outlook was cloudy at best on him reuniting with Johnson.</p><p>Yet there seemed to be a reckoning among Swift, Johnson and former running backs coach Eric Bieniemy. Swift had looked too shifty, too prone to running horizontally while hunting big plays behind a bad offensive line — until Bieniemy sharpened him with his mantra to “get 4½ yards” first, then look for more.</p><p>Johnson shares Swift’s belief that every play call can turn into a touchdown.</p><p>“He’s willing to go for those hard yards,” Johnson said with pride Sunday after a game in which Swift lost yardage on only one carry.</p><p>Swift maintains his history with Johnson has been all positive and frequently has characterized Johnson as a brilliant play designer with a tenacious personality. On Friday, after signing a three-year, $33.8 million extension that begins next season, Swift expressed how thankful he was “to stick around this group of guys . . . and work alongside Ben.”</p><p>Do they understand each other better now compared to four years ago in Detroit?</p><p>“That’s a good way to put it,” Swift said. “I take a lot of pride in making sure my coach is able to trust me.”</p><p>That’s uncommon humility for such a talented player. Had the Bears cut Swift this year to save salary-cap money, he would have found a new home in a minute — everyone in the NFL knows how good he is. But he and Johnson know something, too: how much they can elevate each other. And that makes bending toward the other completely worth it.</p>

entries.title: Boy, 17, accused of shooting pregnant teen in Little Village
entries.summary: <p>A 17-year-old boy is accused of shooting and seriously injuring a pregnant 16-year-old girl he is acquainted with during an argument earlier this month in Little Village.</p><p>The teen, who is not being identified, was cited in a juvenile petition with felony aggravated battery and misdemeanor unlawful use of a weapon, Chicago police said in a statement. <br>He is scheduled to appear in Juvenile Court on Tuesday. </p><p>He was arrested Monday in the 2000 block of South California Avenue after he was identified as person who shot a 16-year-old pregnant girl who he knows during a quarrel on Sept. 7 in the 2200 block of South Sawyer Avenue. </p><p>She suffered at least one gunshot wound to the back and was taken in serious condition to Mount Sinai Hospital, police said at the time. <br></p>

entries.title: Victim killed in Humboldt Park mass shooting identified as Austin neighborhood teen
entries.summary: <p>A man who was killed Sunday afternoon during a mass shooting that left at least six other people injured in Humboldt Park Sunday afternoon has been identified as an Austin neighborhood resident, Chicago police said.</p><p>Seven people were standing outside at about 12:17 p.m. near an alley along the 700 block of North Christiana Avenue when two unknown vehicles approached and multiple armed people exited the vehicles and fired shots, according to police.</p><p>Michael Howard, 18, suffered multiple gunshot wounds and taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office, which ruled the Austin man's death a homicide. </p><p>Six others wounded including a 14-year-old boy and a woman, police said. <br></p><ul id="rte-9e8fbca2-b10c-11f1-b680-ef87d506be8b"><li>A 24-year-old man was shot in the leg and stomach and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was initially reported to be in critical condition. </li><li>A 14-year-old boy suffered gunshot wounds to his thighs and was taken to Stroger Hospital. entries.title: Connor Bedard is now Blackhawks' captain, best player and face of franchise, all in one
entries.summary: <p>From a marketing standpoint, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> have been Connor Bedard's team for three years already. </p><p>He became the face of the franchise the moment he was drafted in June 2023 — perhaps even dating back a month further, to the moment the Hawks won the draft lottery in May 2023. Nothing about his performance since has changed that fact.</p><p>Now, the Hawks are officially Bedard's team — in the locker room, in the NHL's roster logs and more. </p><p>The Hawks named the 21-year-old star the 37th captain in franchise history Tuesday, following most recently Jonathan Toews (2008-2023) and Nick Foligno (2024-2026). He becomes the youngest captain in the league.</p><p>"Being named captain of the Blackhawks is an unbelievable honor and something I'm truly humbled by," Bedard said in a statement. "The captains who have come before me have left an incredible legacy. To now have the opportunity to carry that tradition forward is something I don't take lightly.</p><p>"I'm grateful to the organization and my teammates for putting their trust in me to lead this team. We're building something really special here, and I'm committed to making the entire Blackhawks organization and our fans proud."</p><p>The announcement was hardly surprising. The progression from Foligno's bridge captaincy to Bedard's long-term captaincy always seemed preordained, and that's exactly how it played out — just with a few months separating their tenures.</p><p>Bedard openly discussed his readiness to wear the "C" during exit interviews last April, further cementing the inevitability.</p><p>It's common in the modern NHL for teams' best players to also serve as their captains, regardless of age. Foligno represented an exception to that trend. Bedard fits it perfectly, falling in with the likes of Connor McDavid (Oilers), Auston Matthews (Maple Leafs), Nick Suzuki (Canadiens) and Clayton Keller (Mammoth).</p><p>Bedard's production has cemented his cornerstone status, even if frustratingly little team success has come from it to so far. He has 203 points in 219 games over his first three seasons, matching Patrick Kane's production in his first 219 games. No other Hawk has tallied more than 122 points over the last three seasons combined.</p><p>Bedard checked another prerequisite box by signing a five-year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/18/connor-bedard-blackhawks-new-contract-nhl-free-agency" target="_blank" >contract</a> this summer. General manager Kyle Davidson pushed Bedard to accept a medium-length term to send a message about his commitment to the organization. That idea resonated with Bedard, and he accepted.</p><p>Maturity and leadership skills still matter, though, even if they're not the sole determining factors of captaincy the way they might've been decades ago.</p><p>And in that regard, Bedard's growth — particularly over the last 12 months — checked the final box to demonstrate he's ready for the captaincy. He revealed a more comfortable, outspoken and occasionally funny side of himself last season, allowing his genuine <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/10/29/connor-bedard-blackhawks-voice-honest-kings-boring-macklin-celebrini?_gl=1*1twna7a*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTE0Mjc3NjY2Mi4xNzg5NDE2Mzc4*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODk0MTYzNzgkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODk0MTYzNzgkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >personality</a> and his public persona to become one.</p><p>"When you first get [into the NHL], you're not paranoid, but you don't want to say something that might rub people the wrong way or make me look bad," Bedard told the Sun-Times last October.</p><p>"Obviously I don't want to look bad, but I don't really care too much about what some people think. And I think it's good for the fans if we can show a little bit of who we are, in some ways."</p><p>Behind closed doors, he has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/16/connor-bedard-blackhawks-captain-ready-leadership-alex-vlasic" target="_blank" >proven to peers</a> he's ready to handle the pressure accompanying this role and, in doing so, guide the team out of its long, painful rebuild.</p><p>"He's the perfect guy for [the captaincy]," Ryan Greene said in April. "He cares about his teammates and checks in on everybody all the time. He's our guy. So he's leading the way in a lot of different ways. I think he's more than ready."</p><p>Said Ryan Donato: "I've seen how [Connor has] changed as a person and player, and he's shown everybody in this organization — including me — that he knows what it takes to win. He's put in the work. He's dedicated. And obviously he's the franchise player."</p><p>Following Tuesday's announcement, the Bedard intrigue shifts to his rehab from left shoulder surgery in July. It seems to be progressing nicely, as he has been skating on his own and doing some light shooting for the past week or two.</p><p><i>This story will be updated.</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago man charged after boy fires gun on school bus in Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man was charged after a boy fired a gun on a school bus Monday afternoon in Bridgeport on the South Side. </p><p>Steven Dixon Jr., 22, was charged with a felony count of possessing or carrying a firearm on school property and misdemeanor counts of child endangerment and reckless conduct, Chicago police said. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/14/boy-gun-school-bus-bridgeport" target="_blank" >Dixon Jr., of Chicago, allegedly left a bag on a bus </a>around 2:25 p.m. Monday in the 3500 block of South Wallace Street when a 12-year-old boy found the bag, took a firearm out of it and fired one round, police said. </p><p>Dixon Jr. then allegedly took the bag and fled, officials said. No injuries were reported. </p><p>Dixon Jr. was expected to appear in court Tuesday. </p>
